# Panel Specificity Validation — README

Companion notebook: `07_Panel_Specificity_Validation.ipynb`

## What this notebook is for

Confirms that the final 3-gene panel — **HERC5, BATF2, SPATS2L** — tracks
SLE status, and not pregnancy complication severity, pregnancy status
alone, or technical batch. Two focused questions, one consistent
statistical framework, covering only the 3 genes that made the final
panel. Headings and structure follow the same conventions as
`05_Batch_Effect_Analysis.ipynb` (Track C) — `## Title`, numbered
`### STEP N: ...` sections, `INPUT_DIR` + `os.path.join(...)` paths, and
the same aligned-constant style.

## Design decisions and why

| Decision | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Genes tested | Only HERC5, BATF2, SPATS2L | The other 12 bootstrap-stable genes aren't in the final panel |
| Custom functions (`def`) | None | Matches the thesis's established code style |
| SLE vs. Healthy overall | Not re-tested | Already established on the full transcriptome in the primary DE/ML pipeline (phases `[04]`/`[05]`) — see the explicit `# NOTE:` comment in Step 1 |
| Test statistic | Likelihood-ratio test (LRT), consistently, for both models | More reliable than a Wald test in small/moderate samples; extends cleanly to a multi-level predictor (`complication_group`, 3 levels) in one omnibus step |
| Timepoint | Dropped from both models | Simplifies the models without changing what they're built to detect |
| Batch | Adjusted for directly, as a covariate, in **both** models | See the full rationale below |
| Complication-group derivation | Computed inline (no function), same PE→OC→NC logic as Track A and Track C's Step 9 | Self-contained; matches Hong et al.'s own criteria |
| Multiple-testing correction | 2 independent families (complication specificity, pregnancy specificity), BH-FDR across 3 genes each — 6 tests total | Each family is a genuinely different biological question |
| Expression inputs | 2 files, merged (see below) | No single unzipped file covers all 498 samples — see "Why two expression files" |
| Metadata input | 1 file, your full metadata | Already covers all 498 samples including the 23 NP donors |
| Outputs | 3 CSVs (one per model, one combined) + 3 plots (one per model's grouping variable, plus batch) | Each numeric result has a visual counterpart, not just batch |

## Why two expression files instead of one

There's no single unzipped file that covers all 498 samples together — the
combined raw matrix only exists inside a zip archive, which this notebook
avoids using. Instead, Step 1 loads two flat files that together cover
every sample the pipeline uses:

- `00_expression_NP_only_locked.tsv` — 13,416 genes × 23 samples (the
  never-pregnant donors, unfiltered)
- `00_final_filtered_expression_non_NP_donors.tsv` — 9,055 genes × 475
  samples (the pregnant-cohort donors, post-QC)

Step 2 restricts each to the 3 final-panel genes, transposes both from
genes-as-rows to samples-as-rows, and concatenates them into one combined
expression table before merging with metadata. This is a storage/upload
constraint, not a methodological choice — the two files are two halves of
one original matrix (their GEO sample IDs, `GSM...`, run on sequentially
from one file into the other), split apart because the variance/
low-expression filter was only ever computed on the non-NP training set
(per the project's methodology notes).

## Why batch is adjusted for directly, in both models

**Complication status is confirmed to exist only for SLE donors.** Checked
directly against the source paper (Hong et al., 2019, *J Exp Med*):
complications (NC=46, PE=24, OC=22, summing to the 92 SLE-pregnant donors)
are only ever assigned within "pregnant SLE patients." Healthy participants
were pre-screened specifically to be low-risk, so complication status was
never a meaningful thing to assign them. This means Model 1 (SLE-only)
doesn't confound `complication_group` with `Condition` inside the model
itself — `Condition` is fixed at SLE for every row there.

**What that doesn't rule out is batch.** Track C's own whole-transcriptome
analysis already found batch comparable in size to Condition on PC4 of a
PCA — batch and biology are not fully independent in this dataset. If a
batch happens to overlap disproportionately with, say, the PE donors
specifically, an unadjusted complication test could mistake that processing
difference for a complication effect — or the reverse, mask a real one.

**Folding batch into the same model as the predictor of interest** — rather
than testing it separately, as Track C's Step 7 does for the 15-gene set —
is the standard way to handle exactly this situation:

1. **Leek, J.T., Scharpf, R.B., Bravo, H.C., et al. (2010). "Tackling the
   widespread and critical impact of batch effects in high-throughput
   data." *Nature Reviews Genetics*, 11(10), 733–739.
   https://doi.org/10.1038/nrg2825** — batch effects become dangerous
   specifically when they correlate with the outcome under study.
2. **Johnson, W.E., Li, C., & Rabinovic, A. (2007). "Adjusting batch
   effects in microarray expression data using empirical Bayes methods."
   *Biostatistics*, 8(1), 118–127. https://doi.org/10.1093/biostatistics/kxj037**
   — the ComBat paper, directly relevant since GSE108497 is Illumina
   microarray data. Their method keeps the biological variable of interest
   in the same model used to estimate the batch term, so real biology
   isn't stripped out along with the technical noise.

## What is a likelihood-ratio test (LRT)?

An LRT compares two *nested* models — a "full" model with the predictor of
interest, and a "reduced" model without it — by asking how much better the
full model explains the data:
`2 × (full model's log-likelihood − reduced model's log-likelihood)`
follows a chi-squared distribution under "the predictor doesn't matter,"
with degrees of freedom equal to how many extra parameters the full model
has. Used consistently for both models, rather than mixing in a simpler
Wald test for one — Wald tests are less reliable in small/moderate samples
and don't extend as cleanly to a multi-level predictor.

## Required inputs

Three files, all plain/flat — no zip archives needed. **Confirm the exact
paths and column names in Step 1 before running.**

### Expression (2 files, merged in Step 2)
- `00_expression_NP_only_locked.tsv` — genes as rows, 23 NP samples as columns
- `00_final_filtered_expression_non_NP_donors.tsv` — genes as rows, 475 samples as columns

### Metadata (1 file, your full metadata)
Covers all 498 samples:

| Notebook variable | Default column guess | What it needs to contain |
|---|---|---|
| `sample_id` | `Sample` | Joins to the expression files (matches Track C's convention) |
| `donor_id` | `Donor_id` | Random-intercept grouping variable |
| `Condition` | `Condition` | `SLE` / `Healthy` |
| `pregnancy_status` | `pregnancy_status` | e.g. `Pregnant` / `NP` — **not directly observed in Track C**, which instead derives NP status from a missing `time_point` (`fillna("NP")`); use that same rule if your metadata lacks this column |
| `batch` | `batch` | Same batch variable used in Track C |
| `pe`, `fd`, `nnd`, `pl_insuff`, `iugr`, `sga` | same names | Raw adverse-outcome flags (SLE donors only), same as Track A and Track C. `apl`/`lac` are excluded — not part of this grouping |

If your actual column names differ, update the `..._COL` variables in
Step 1 — nothing else needs to change.

## Workflow — what happens, step by step

- **STEP 0 — Install packages.** Same as Track C: a commented `%pip
  install` line, safe to run every time.
- **STEP 1 — Data input.** Sets `INPUT_DIR`, imports, defines file paths
  (aligned constants, same style as Track C), creates `OUTPUT_DIR`, loads
  both expression files and the metadata file, asserts all 3 genes are
  present in both expression files, prints shapes. Carries the `# NOTE:`
  explaining why SLE vs. Healthy isn't re-tested.
- **STEP 2 — Combine expression files and merge with metadata.**
  Transposes and concatenates the two expression files, merges with
  metadata on `sample_id`, prints the donor-level 92/43/23 sanity check.
- **Why batch is adjusted for / What is an LRT** — rationale cells, no
  numbered step, matching Track C's own "Why...?" header pattern.
- **STEP 3 — Complication-group derivation.** Inline PE→OC→NC logic for
  SLE donors, prints the 46/24/22 sanity check.
- **STEP 4 — Model 1 (complication specificity).** Cross-tab check, then
  full vs. reduced mixed models per gene, LRT, BH-FDR. Saves
  `model1_complication_specificity.csv`.
- **STEP 5 — Model 2 (pregnancy specificity).** Same procedure, Healthy
  donors only, `pregnancy_status` instead of `complication_group`. Saves
  `model2_pregnancy_specificity.csv`.
- **STEP 6 — Combined results.** Stacks both models, adds a per-gene
  pass/flag summary. Saves `combined_results.csv`.
- **STEP 7 — Three visual counterparts, one per grouping variable.**
  Plot 1: per-gene expression by batch, colored by Condition (all 498
  samples) — saves `panel_by_batch.png`. Plot 2: per-gene expression by
  complication group (SLE donors only) — saves
  `panel_by_complication_group.png`. Plot 3: per-gene expression by
  pregnancy status (Healthy donors only) — saves
  `panel_by_pregnancy_status.png`. None are statistical tests; each cell
  can be deleted independently.
- **STEP 8 — Interpret results.** Limitations and what's intentionally
  excluded, same closing pattern as Track A/B/C.

## How to read the results

A gene is "specific to SLE" if its FDR-corrected p-value is
**non-significant (> 0.05) in both** rows.

## Results (from the real run)

The notebook produces four files. Each is shown below with what it
actually says.

### `combined_results.csv`

| Gene | Test | Raw p-value | FDR-corrected p-value |
|---|---|---|---|
| BATF2 | complication specificity | 0.296 | 0.443 |
| BATF2 | pregnancy specificity | 0.169 | 0.253 |
| HERC5 | complication specificity | 0.801 | 0.801 |
| HERC5 | pregnancy specificity | 0.667 | 0.667 |
| SPATS2L | complication specificity | 0.066 | 0.197 |
| SPATS2L | pregnancy specificity | 0.121 | 0.253 |

This is the single table that answers the notebook's whole question: all
six FDR-corrected p-values sit above 0.05, so none of HERC5, BATF2, or
SPATS2L show evidence of tracking complication severity or pregnancy
status once SLE status and batch are accounted for — the panel's
SLE-vs-Healthy signal isn't attributable to either confound in this
cohort. SPATS2L's complication-specificity row is the one worth reading
carefully rather than glossing over: its raw p-value (0.066) sits close
enough to 0.05 that it should be described in the thesis as "no evidence
of an effect after FDR correction," not as a comfortably settled null the
way the other five rows are.

### `model1_complication_specificity.csv`

| Gene | Raw p-value | FDR-corrected p-value |
|---|---|---|
| HERC5 | 0.801 | 0.801 |
| BATF2 | 0.296 | 0.443 |
| SPATS2L | 0.066 | 0.197 |

Model 1 on its own — whether expression differs across NC/PE/OC within SLE
donors, batch-adjusted. Same conclusion as the complication rows above:
nothing survives FDR correction, so the panel doesn't appear to be
tracking complication severity rather than SLE itself. SPATS2L is the one
gene here whose raw p-value would have been nominally noteworthy before
correction — worth a one-line mention in the thesis discussion as a
direction to watch in a larger cohort, not as a finding on its own.

### `model2_pregnancy_specificity.csv`

| Gene | Raw p-value | FDR-corrected p-value |
|---|---|---|
| HERC5 | 0.667 | 0.667 |
| BATF2 | 0.169 | 0.253 |
| SPATS2L | 0.121 | 0.253 |

Model 2 on its own — whether expression differs between Healthy-Pregnant
and Healthy-Never-Pregnant donors, batch-adjusted. All three raw p-values
sit comfortably above 0.05, with no borderline case this time (BATF2's and
SPATS2L's FDR values are tied at 0.253 simply because BH-FDR ties the two
smallest p-values when they're close together — not because of anything
special about either gene). This is the cleaner of the two specificity
checks: nothing here suggests the panel is picking up pregnancy status
rather than SLE.

### `panel_by_batch.png`

![Final 3-gene panel, expression by batch, colored by Condition](data:image/png;base64,)

This plot is what makes the batch-adjustment rationale earlier in this
README concrete rather than hypothetical. Batch 3 is visibly almost all
blue (Healthy) across all three genes — consistent with Track C's own
finding that batch 3 is 44 of 45 Healthy samples, with only a single SLE
sample in it. That's a real, visible batch/condition imbalance, exactly
the kind that could let a processing artifact masquerade as a disease
signal if left unadjusted. The fact that both specificity models still
come out non-significant *after* adjusting for this confound is more
reassuring than a null result would have been from a dataset where batch
and Condition were already independent of each other.

### `panel_by_complication_group.png`

![Final 3-gene panel, SLE donors only, by complication group](data:image/png;base64,)

The direct visual counterpart to Model 1. Same story as the p-values: no
gene shows a clean separation across NC/PE/OC. SPATS2L's boxes shift
slightly upward from NC through PE to OC — consistent with it being the
one borderline result in the table above (raw p=0.066) — but the spread
within each group is large enough relative to that shift that it isn't a
visually obvious effect either. HERC5 and BATF2 show essentially flat
medians across all three groups.

### `panel_by_pregnancy_status.png`

![Final 3-gene panel, Healthy donors only, by pregnancy status](data:image/png;base64,)

### Are the three genes expected to move together across complication groups?

Not automatically — if the three genes were independent, unrelated
measurements, there would be no particular reason for all three to shift
the same direction from NC through PE to OC. Seeing them agree is not a
given.

It is not surprising for this specific panel, though. HERC5, BATF2, and
SPATS2L were not selected independently — they were selected together
specifically because they behave similarly across SLE vs. Healthy, and
per the Track B literature review, HERC5 and BATF2 in particular are
general type I interferon markers rather than narrowly SLE-specific ones.
Genes on the same biological axis tend to move together: if any shared
factor nudges expression up slightly in PE/OC donors relative to NC — not
necessarily anything complication-specific — all three genes would
plausibly drift the same direction together, simply because they are
reading out the same underlying signal.

A concrete candidate for that shared factor comes directly from the
source paper: Hong et al. report that baseline disease activity (SLEPDAI)
differs by complication group — SLE-PE averaged 4.43, SLE-OC 2.86,
SLE-NC 2.35 (their own P=0.026). Disease activity tracks the type I
interferon response, which is exactly what these three genes are
reading. So a small, same-direction shift across all three genes — with
none of them individually clearing significance — is consistent with
"PE/OC donors happened to have slightly higher baseline disease activity
in this cohort," rather than with any complication-specific biology.

This is a useful framing for the thesis discussion section: the
consistent direction across genes doesn't strengthen the case that
complication status itself is driving expression (the FDR-corrected test
already says it isn't), but it does suggest the borderline SPATS2L result
is more likely a faint echo of general disease activity than noise in one
gene alone — worth a sentence in the discussion, not a finding, and not
something that changes any code or numbers in this notebook.

## What's deliberately not in here

- **SLE vs. Healthy overall** — already established in the primary DE/ML
  pipeline.
- **The other 12 bootstrap-stable genes** — out of scope for the final panel.
- **Track C's whole-transcriptome PCA/UMAP battery and standalone batch
  test** — batch is addressed inline as a covariate above instead.
- **The pooled three-group pregnancy model** — its only other job was
  re-deriving the SLE-vs-Healthy effect, already covered by the primary
  pipeline, and it carried an unresolved variance-pooling artifact this
  design sidesteps entirely.

## Limitations

Donor random-intercept covariance (vs. Hong et al.'s spatial-power
structure) and the LRT's chi-squared approximation are both slightly
anti-conservative in general — this doesn't threaten the conclusions here
specifically, since both models are built to detect a null result. Batch
adjustment guards against complication/pregnancy status being confounded
with processing batch; it doesn't establish that `batch` fully captures
every source of technical variation in the dataset.
